Achieving self-sufficiency in China's future maize production through data-driven interpretable machine learning strategies
Coupling agroclimatic indices and species distribution models to project future plum-growing zones in Morocco
From adoption to adaptation: Smallholder decision logics behind the irrigation adoption paradox
The Daisy model: A tool for simulating agricultural systems – Recent (2012–2025) developments, calibrations and validations
abstract: CONTEXT Process-based agroecological models are essential tools for understanding and managing agroecosystems. The agroecological model Daisy is widely used across climates and farming systems to simulate crop growth, water and heat dynamics, carbon turnover, nutrient cycling, and pollutant leaching. OBJECTIVE This paper documents Daisy's developments since 2012, evaluates its performance in peer-reviewed studies, and outlines priorities for future development. METHODS We describe the bioclimate, vegetation, and soil modules, including submodules for water flow, heat transport, organic matter dynamics, and solute transport, covering nitrogen dynamics and pesticide fate. We also review approximately 120 peer-reviewed studies published between 2012 and 2025 in which Daisy was applied. In addition, we introduce new tools for calibration, parallel execution, and output visualization, and outline future needs such as improved modelling of dissolved organic matter, a gas-transport module, and enhanced representation of soil structural dynamics and their effects on hydraulic properties. RESULTS AND CONCLUSSIONS Key new extensions include a model for preferential water flow and pesticide transport in vertically oriented biopores, simulations of natural toxin generation and wash-off, and an air–water interface and sorption model essential for PFAS fate assessment. Ongoing developments address surface plant residue dynamics, N₂O emissions, and dynamic soil structure changes. The literature review confirms Daisy's robust performance in simulating water balance, crop production, nitrogen cycling (including nitrate leaching), carbon sequestration, and the fate of natural and anthropogenic chemicals across diverse climates, soils, and management systems. SIGNIFICANCE Daisy remains a strong model for advancing process understanding and supporting scenario analysis to promote sustainable agricultural production.

title: Village-level multi-objective optimization of wheat and maize area constraints: Balancing irrigation water use, carbon intensity, and farm income
A framework for conceptualizing agricultural diversification with a focus on the U.S. Corn Belt
abstract: CONTEXT Diversification of agricultural production has been proposed to address interrelated social, ecological, and economic challenges. However, definitions of agricultural diversification vary, and there has been negligible research documenting what farmers consider to be diversification. A shared understanding of agricultural diversification is needed to create common goals and support policies and programs that incorporate the vision of the agriculture community. OBJECTIVE We examine the meaning of agricultural diversification according to agricultural stakeholders with a focus on the U.S. Corn Belt. METHODS Data on farmer understandings of diversification from focus groups ( n = 20 groups) and a survey ( n = 725 respondents) across the U.S. states of Iowa, Illinois, and Indiana are compared to 1) a review of definitions of agricultural diversification found in academic and grey literature and 2) a definition created by a team of academics, Extension, and non-governmental professionals. RESULTS And CONCLUSION Five dimensions of agricultural diversity emerged: biological, economic, human, values, and cognitive. Across sources, diversification is typically discussed in biological and economic terms. Some sources mention values of conservation or sustainability as components of agricultural diversification and relatively fewer identify human dimensions. While the cognitive dimension of diversification did not emerge in the literature review, it was mentioned frequently by focus group participants. SIGNIFICANCE We provide a framework for understanding agricultural diversification and propose future efforts in this area define how the term is used across each of the five dimensions. Future outreach activities can leverage aspects of diversification that are compelling and achievable to farmers.

title: Integrated soil-water-fertilizer synergetic strategy for sustainable vegetable production: Advancing food-energy-water‑carbon nexus in Southern China
Multi-objective optimization of wheat-maize management for climate-smart agriculture in China
Conservation agriculture in Argentina and Germany: a comparative review of adoption pathways and environmental outcomes
abstract: Context Conservation Agriculture (CA), defined by minimal mechanical soil disturbance, permanent soil organic cover, and species diversification, has been proposed as a systems-based pathway toward sustainable intensification. Argentina and Germany represent different agricultural, socio-economic, and institutional contexts across Latin America and Europe, offering an opportunity to analyze how CA principles are interpreted and implemented, across distinct developmental trajectories. Objective This review synthesizes evidence on CA adoption pathways and environmental outcomes in both countries, distinguishing between the adoption of individual CA principles and fully integrated CA systems, as well as between environmental effects associated with agricultural expansion and those related to management changes within already established cropping systems. Methods A systematic literature review was conducted following PRISMA guidelines to assess CA outcomes on soil health, carbon dynamics, water regulation, greenhouse gas emissions, pest and weed management, and biodiversity. Additional literature was analyzed to contextualize agricultural development trajectories and CA adoption dynamics. Results and conclusions The existing literature reveals both converging and diverging patterns in implementation of CA principles, strongly shaped by distinct agricultural development trajectories. In Argentina, no-tillage adoption emerged primarily as a response to soil degradation within a broader technological and economic expansion process. In Germany, CA practices are mainly implemented as management adjustments within long-established cropping systems, emphasizing reduced tillage, diversification, and environmental compliance. In both countries, simultaneous implementation of all three CA principles remains limited and environmental outcomes are strongly context-dependent. Significance By linking CA adoption pathways to historical development trajectories, this review provides a context-sensitive assessment of CA performance relevant for researchers, practitioners, and policymakers designing sustainable intensification strategies.

title: Grazing re-engineers the plant-animal-soil carbon pump across topographic gradients
Assessing the relationship between structural characteristics, profitability, and extra-financial performance in a French pig farming network
abstract: CONTEXT The French pig farming sector faces dual economic and societal pressures, driving a transformation in production models. To ensure long-term viability, farms must increasingly reconcile economic competitiveness with societal expectations, proxied in this study through audit-based extra-financial indicators (animal welfare and Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) scores). OBJECTIVE This study explores the structural factors associated with this multidimensional performance within a selected cooperative network. METHODS Relying on a techno-economic database spanning from 1995 to 2024, we analyzed structural evolutions, modeled an experience curve, and assessed the cross-sectional associations between farm size and investment levels in 2024. RESULTS AND CONCLUSIONS Longitudinal results confirm a structural trend toward concentration (+43% sows per farm on average) and increased capital intensity. Fitting a learning curve suggests that a doubling of cumulative production is associated with a 9% reduction in inflation-adjusted added costs, representing a composite effect of both organizational learning and sector-wide technological adoption. The comparative analysis of 204 farms in 2024 reveals that investment capacity is strongly correlated with overall performance. Farms in the top investment quintile are larger (+108%), more profitable (recalculated EBITDA/sow +78%), and score better on animal welfare (+10%) and CSR (+18%). SIGNIFICANCE Multivariate models confirm that investment level, rather than farm size alone, is a significant predictor of these outcomes. However, these results identify associations rather than causal mechanisms. Furthermore, the modest share of variance explained by the structural models (R² = 0.17 to 0.20) highlights that the vast majority of performance differences remains strongly associated with non-structural elements, notably the 'human factor' and individual managerial quality.

title: Mixed-cropping enhances profitability and reduces greenhouse gas emissions in semi-arid dryland cropping regions
Public land grazing simplifies grassland multifunctionality: A systemic decoupling of plant-soil interactions in a temperate pastoral system
Spatio-temporal analysis for identifying hotspots and trends of nitrogen and potential energy valorisation from livestock manure in Italy
abstract: Context Managing livestock manure is a key sustainability challenge because it represents both a source of nutrient pollution and a resource for renewable energy production. In Italy, the spatial concentration of livestock systems generates heterogeneous patterns of nitrogen pressure and energy potential, requiring targeted, spatially explicit policy approaches. Objective This study uses a GIS-based spatio-temporal framework to quantify nitrogen loads and manure-derived energy potential at the municipal level in Italy. The aim is to identify environmental and energy hotspots and assess the trajectory of the livestock sector up to 2026. Methods Municipal-level livestock data for cattle, buffalo, and pigs (2011−2023) were integrated with geospatial datasets and analysed using spatial statistics and spatio-temporal pattern mining. Spatial clustering was assessed using local indicators (Getis–Ord Gi*), while temporal dynamics were captured through a space-time cube framework. Nitrogen loads and energy potential were estimated using standardised coefficients, and forecasting models were applied to project herd and farm trends up to 2026, assuming that historical trends represent short-term future dynamics Results and conclusions The results reveal clear spatial patterns in nitrogen pressure and energy potential. There are persistent and emerging hotspots, which are mainly concentrated in northern Italy and partially overlap with Nitrate Vulnerable Zones. Areas with high livestock density demonstrate the greatest potential for biogas production, which confirms the spatial relationship between nutrient surpluses and opportunities for energy recovery. Temporal analysis indicates a general decline in cattle and pig herds and holdings, alongside a localized increase in buffalo farming, particularly in Campania and Lazio. Forecast results suggest continued restructuring of the sector, with an estimated 27% reduction in the number of farms between 2011 and 2026, primarily impacting small and medium-sized holdings. These findings highlight the spatial reorganisation of livestock systems, with environmental pressures and energy opportunities becoming increasingly concentrated in the intensive livestock regions of northern Italy, particularly in the Po Valley and parts of Piedmont, as well as in the buffalo-farming areas of Campania and Lazio. The proposed framework shows how combining spatial, temporal and predictive analyses can help identify critical and opportunity areas for targeted policy interventions. Significance The results highlight areas of high nitrogen pressure and energy potential, as well as short-term structural changes in the livestock sector. By integrating spatial, temporal, and predictive analyses within a single framework, the proposed approach provides a comprehensive assessment that supports the identification of critical and opportunity areas for targeted interventions.

title: Towards a resilience framework for Australian extensive cattle systems facing increasing climate extremes: A review
abstract: CONTEXT Extreme weather events, particularly heatwaves, droughts, floods, and wildfires, increasingly threaten extensive cattle systems. These events intensify heat stress (HS), increase the risk of disease outbreaks, disrupt feedbase productivity and quality, reduce forage availability, and constrain water resources. These climate-related stressors cumulatively impair productivity, reproductive performance, and animal welfare, with important implications for the long-term sustainability of extensive cattle production. OBJECTIVE This review evaluates the effects of climatic extremes on extensive cattle systems and proposes a systems-level resilience framework for extensive beef production, emphasising the integration of real-time HS monitoring, adaptive grazing management, and data-driven approaches to identify resilient animals and inform breeding strategies. METHODS A structured narrative review was conducted to identify and synthesise evidence on climate-related stressors, feedbase dynamics, grazing management, cattle monitoring technologies, and data-driven approaches relevant to the development of a systems-level resilience framework for extensive cattle systems under climate extremes. RESULTS AND CONCLUSIONS A systems-level, three-pillar framework is proposed to enhance resilience and productivity in extensive cattle systems: (1) real-time HS monitoring using physiological, behavioural, and environmental indicators; (2) adaptive grazing and feedbase diversification strategies to sustain forage quality and availability; and (3) data-driven approaches that integrate climate, feedbase, and production metrics to identify resilient animals and inform breeding strategies. Practical implementation in pasture-based systems can be supported by precision livestock farming technologies, including advanced HS monitoring tools, adaptive grazing management, and automated in-field weighing. SIGNIFICANCE The framework facilitates continuous animal-level assessment in extensive cattle systems, supports proactive responses to extreme weather events and climate variability, and contributes to sustaining productivity, animal welfare, and long-term herd resilience.

title: Scale-dependent effects of area and spatial heterogeneity on crop diversity and nutrient productivity in Latin America
Scaling through friction: Learning, trust, and institutional alignment in global AgTech
abstract: CONTEXT Agri-technology (AgTech) ventures are often portrayed as globally scalable solutions for transforming food systems, yet agriculture differs from other technology domains in its dependence on local ecological, institutional, and social contexts. Standard internationalization models - such as born global and international new ventures -assume scalability through replication, but AgTech ventures must engage with diversity, not overcome it. OBJECTIVE This study introduces the concept of context-responsive scaling to explain how AgTech ventures expand across heterogeneous agricultural systems. It explores how firms convert ecological and institutional friction into learning and legitimacy, proposing a framework that connects firm-level adaptation with responsible and transformative scaling in food systems. METHODS The research draws on 48 semi-structured interviews with AgTech founders, investors, and ecosystem actors across Asia, Africa, Latin America, and Europe, complemented by field notes and documentary evidence. Using grounded theorizing, it identifies recurrent practices through which firms translate technologies, build trust, and co-shape institutional environments. RESULTS AND CONCLUSIONS AgTech ventures scale not by removing friction but by learning through it. They develop three interlinked dynamic capabilities: contextual translation (making technology meaningful in local farming logics), relational intermediation (building legitimacy through trusted intermediaries), and institutional co-shaping (engaging in rule-making and alignment with public goals). These capabilities enable distributed learning systems that reconcile global coherence with local embeddedness. SIGNIFICANCE The study reframes scaling as an interpretive, relational, and ethical process. It conceptualizes embeddedness as a dynamic capability and connects organizational learning to system transformation. For practice, it calls for scaling programs that reward co-creation, partnership depth, and institutional learning rather than rapid replication. Scaling through friction thus represents a transformative pathway for more resilient and inclusive agri-food innovation.

title: Cost-effective urban farming with alternative water sources treated by nature-based solutions: A critical review of global practices
abstract: Urban agriculture supports food security and circular resource use in cities, yet expansion is hindered by limited clean irrigation water. This review examines five alternative water sources available in urban environments (i.e., greywater, blackwater, groundwater, rainwater, and stormwater) for urban crop irrigation, assessing their agronomic suitability and contaminant profiles through systematic global literature synthesis. Four nature-based solution (NBS) technologies (i.e., constructed wetlands, biofilters, green roofs, and green walls) were evaluated as pre-treatment systems, alongside international regulatory frameworks and an economic model applied to tomatoes, faba beans, and sweet peppers. Each water source presents a distinct risk-benefit profile, with contaminants spanning nutrients, pathogens, heavy metals, and emerging pollutants. NBS technologies effectively reduce these risks while retaining crop-beneficial nutrients, with hybrid systems such as wetland-biofilter combinations achieved removal efficiencies exceeding 97% for TSS, BOD, and COD. Crop selection was decisive for economic viability, with high-value crops such as tomatoes and sweet peppers irrigated with treated groundwater yielded the greatest profitability, while faba beans remained unviable regardless of treatment approach. Policy analysis identified substantial governance gaps, including inconsistent enforcement, limited public acceptance, and minimal regulatory guidance specific to urban agricultural water reuse. By integrating treatment technology, crop suitability, economic viability, and policy considerations into a unified framework, this review demonstrates that alternative water sources can meaningfully advance food security and support multiple Sustainable Development Goals when appropriate safeguards are in place.

title: Livestock farming intensification: Mitigating or exacerbating feed-food competition? Contrasting results in broiler, dairy, and beef production
abstract: Context Feed-food competition arises when livestock consume feed and use land that could serve human nutrition directly. Livestock intensification is often considered to improve productivity and resource-use efficiency; however, its impact on feed-food competition remains unclear, particularly across animal products. Objective The aim of this study was to investigate how intensification affects feed-food competition in broiler, dairy and beef commercial farms across Europe classified along a gradient of inputs related to intensification, under the hypothesis that productivity increases with the level of inputs. Methods We used data from 79 broiler, 77 dairy, and 53 beef farms selected across a wide range of farming systems from nine EU countries. We characterised intensification as a set of inputs intended to increase productivity and classified farms into six broiler, seven dairy, and six beef intensification classes. For each farm, we calculated the productivity, the protein feed conversion ratio considering all feeds or only human-edible feeds and the land use considering all land or only arable land. Results and conclusions Results show that intensification improves productivity, and feed and land use efficiencies but gains tend to plateau for high input systems – for example, for feed efficiency at around 2.8, 4.1 and 7.2 kg feed protein/kg protein produced in broilers, dairy and beef, respectively. When considering human-edible protein and arable land, in broilers, indoor systems required half as much resources as outdoor slow growing systems (2.8 vs. 5.0 kg/kg and 27 vs. 57 m 2 /kg). In cattle, strict grass-based systems required almost no human-edible feed protein or arable land, unlike high input systems (0.01 vs. 1.88 kg/kg and 10 vs. 34 m 2 /kg in dairy). Thus, in broilers, intensification mitigates feed-food competition up to a plateau, whereas in cattle, intensification exacerbates it, with grass-based systems even achieving net human-edible protein production. Significance These findings highlight that strategies to reduce feed-food competition appear species-specific and involve livestock intensification in different ways. Supporting grass-based dairy and beef systems, alongside reasonably efficient broiler production, could strengthen food-system sustainability and reduce competition for arable land and human-edible resources. By proposing a multidimensional characterisation of livestock intensification based on farm inputs, this study provides farm-based evidence on the potential and limits of livestock intensification in addressing feed-food competition and in guiding the design of more sustainable livestock systems. However, feed-food competition is only one aspect of sustainability, and broader environmental, economic, and social dimensions must also be considered.

title: Irrigation-induced economic value for global major crops: A biophysical perspective on yield benefits versus greenhouse gas emission costs of croplands
Global synthesis reveals divergent effects of grassland management on ecosystem services
Are agroecological practices pro-poor? Evidence from smallholder farms in Zimbabwe
abstract: CONTEXT Improved farming practices could contribute to solving food insecurity and poverty among smallholder farmers in Zimbabwe, who are dominantly mixed crop-livestock farmers. Agroecological practices, which rely on the use and recycling of local resources to reduce dependency on costly external inputs, are increasingly being claimed as suitable options for resource-constrained farmers. OBJECTIVE The objective of this study was to assess how the use of improved crop and livestock practices, including agroecological ones, varied among different farm types. We hypothesised that agroecological practices would be preferentially used by farms with lower resource-endowment. METHODS Data from a household survey of 605 farms across a representative sub-humid district and a representative semi-arid district in Zimbabwe, documenting the use of 32 common improved crop and livestock practices, 14 of which were classified as agroecological, were used for this study. A farm typology based on practice use was delineated using Multiple Correspondence Analysis, after which the socio-economic characteristics of the farm types and their associations with farm performance were assessed. RESULTS AND CONCLUSIONS Our analysis revealed that farmers using a broader range of improved practices – including agroecological ones – were generally the wealthier and more resource-endowed households. Importantly, we found that these same farms were also more diverse in crop and livestock species, indicating that farm diversity was positively associated with productive capacity and resource endowment, rather than being a compensatory strategy of poorer households. Furthermore, we observed limited and inconsistent associations between the use of improved practices and production or diet outcomes. SIGNIFICANCE The study points to the need for targeted support to less-endowed households, addressing not only technical but also socio-economic and institutional constraints to diversification and the use of improved practices.

title: Impact of 10 years of adaptive multi-paddock grazing on soil carbon and beef's greenhouse gas footprint in the US Upper Midwest
abstract: CONTEXT Adaptive multi-paddock (AMP) grazing has been discussed as an option to reduce beef production's greenhouse gas (GHG) footprint via its potential impacts on soil organic carbon (SOC) accrual. This is especially relevant for the grazing-based cow-calf production phase, responsible for most beef GHGs and where practical mitigation options remain limited. However, existing AMP studies are too few, often short-term, and have key limitations in estimating SOC and GHGs to provide real confidence in its mitigation potential. OBJECTIVE To evaluate decade-scale impacts of AMP grazing on net GHG emissions in beef production systems. METHODS We conducted a life cycle assessment (LCA) using 11 years of on-farm data from an experimental research site in Michigan, USA. We compared two beef production systems, incorporating different combinations of AMP grazing within conventional production phases: AMP-GF (grass-finishing) and AMP-FL (feedlot-finishing), both using AMP grazing for cow-calf and stocker phases. The LCA accounted for all standard GHG sources (i.e., emissions from enteric fermentation, manure management, feed production, on-farm energy use, transportation) and incorporated both measured and modeled SOC change (0–30 cm) over 11 years. RESULTS AND CONCLUSIONS AMP-grazed pastures accrued an estimated 0.52 Mg C ha −1 yr −1 , based on a conservative SOC estimate informed by field measurements and model outputs. Incorporating this SOC change into the LCA reduced net GHG intensities to ∼17 kg CO 2 -e kg CW −1 for both systems, corresponding to 41% (AMP-GF) and 34% (AMP-FL) reductions relative to their baselines. SIGNIFICANCE This study provides rare, decade-scale, system-wide evidence across the full beef lifecycle, showing that AMP grazing can meaningfully mitigate beef GHG emissions through sustained SOC accrual in the Upper Midwest.

title: Optimizing trade-offs and synergies for sustainable intensification: A household-level analysis of mixed farming systems in sub-saharan Africa
New approach to calculate agri-environmental indicators using greenhouse gas emissions in Switzerland as an example
abstract: CONTEXT Agri-environmental monitoring programmes provide policy makers and society with important information on the state of the environment and the achievement of agricultural policy objectives. In this study, we present the new Swiss agri-environmental monitoring programme MAUS (German: “Monitoring des AgrarUmweltsystem Schweiz”) using the indicator of greenhouse gas emissions (GHG) as an example. OBJECTIVE The main objective of this study was to determine GHG emissions for different regions and production systems in Switzerland, thereby demonstrating the feasibility, strengths, and weaknesses of the new monitoring approach MAUS. Furthermore, we aimed to identify the most effective levers for achieving greatest reduction in emissions. METHODS The new monitoring programme approach maximises the use of existing data. To achieve this, it is necessary to compile and link existing data from different sources. An approximate indicator value is calculated for each Swiss farm, and these values are then aggregated to larger scales. To identify the strongest levers for emission reductions, a sensitivity analysis was carried out with three case study farms. RESULTS AND CONCLUSIONS GHG emissions varied spatially across Switzerland, with two hotspot regions of around 7-8 t CO2eq/(ha•yr). A more detailed analysis based on the three case study farms revealed that emissions were mainly driven by livestock numbers. Additional factors driving GHG emissions were feeding intensity, applied commercial fertiliser amount, and pasture time of animals. Other variables, e.g. related to the barn system or the slurry management, had only minor effects on total GHG emissions. MAUS reduces the administrative burden for farmers to deliver data compared to the old monitoring framework, while simultaneously providing flexibility in aggregating the results and a simple framework to integrate additional data sources. However, MAUS requires substantial scientific effort for collating and processing data from multiple organisations and is limited regarding retrospective calculations, thus impeding comparison with previous agri-environmental indicator calculations. SIGNIFICANCEThis study provides decision makers with essential evidence to drive legislation forward by highlighting the regions and key levers where GHG emission reductions can be most effectively achieved. Part of the current agricultural subsidies that aim at reducing GHG emissions are allocated on a per livestock unit basis. Thereby, these subsidies counteract the reduction in livestock numbers and thus the desired reduction in greenhouse gas emissions.

title: Evaluating the yield gap of cropping systems: A comparison of alternative approaches across regions
abstract: CONTEXT Yield gap analyses at the cropping system level are key for identifying opportunities to increase crop yield and support food security globally. While several cropping systems yield gap approaches namely aggregated yield gap, individual crop yield gaps, nutritional, financial, equivalent yield gaps and relative yield gap have been applied in the literature to quantify yield gaps, no studies have reported how different approaches are related or have suggested which metrics are most appropriate for different objectives. OBJECTIVE To address this gap, we evaluated the relationships between those yield gap approaches across different farming systems in two contrasting regions: Queensland, Australia and the dry zone of Sri Lanka. METHODS We evaluated these different approaches using potential crop rotations created using wheat and sorghum in Queensland and rice and mungbean in Sri Lanka. We used the Agricultural Production Systems sIMulator (APSIM) to simulate the yield potential for each cropping system under different sowing windows, planting densities, and cultivars and actual yields were obtained from national statistics reports for the selected regions. RESULTS AND CONCLUSIONS Results revealed a strong correlation between the aggregated yield gap, equivalent yield gap, relative yield gap as well as nutritional and financial yield gaps in both farming systems. However, individual crop yield gaps do not consistently correlate with any of the other approaches suggesting that it is a limited indicator for evaluating the system as a whole in either farming system. This study suggests that the aggregated yield gap is a consistent approach to capture the cropping system performance while requiring minimal data. Relative yield gap reflects system efficiency relative to their potential, making it useful for comparing across crops or cropping systems. SIGNIFICANCE As such, aggregated yield gap is a broadly relevant, valuable yet simple metric for farmers and policymakers to use to improve productivity and food security across farming systems globally.

title: Quantifying ecosystem services under future climate and conservation agriculture scenarios in an agricultural landscape
abstract: Context Agricultural landscapes provide multiple ecosystem services (ES), which are prioritized by different beneficiary communities. Future climate and landscape management choices will result in ecosystem service gains and losses, differentially affecting various beneficiaries. Objective We assessed changes in ES, interactions among ES, and impacts of ES changes on beneficiaries under scenarios representing potential variability in global climate change and regional agroecosystem management. Methods We developed spatially explicit models to quantify the changes in the Montérégie, an agricultural region in Quebec, Canada, for four ecosystem service benefits: corn yield, soil organic carbon, flood control, and sediment control. We estimated ES outcomes by 2050 with a statistical mixed-effects models, InVEST ecosystem service models, and a soil dynamics model. We then quantified relative ES changes and related these changes to affected beneficiaries. Results and conclusions Future scenarios project a 13–16% decline in corn yield, with smaller declines under conservation agriculture scenarios. Water-related ES are projected to decline substantially under extreme climate change, but our models suggest these declines can be largely mitigated by conservation agriculture. Conservation tillage is estimated to increase soil organic carbon storage by 0.14–1.88 tons ha −1 under future climate scenarios. We found an increased trade-off between corn yield and flood control under conservation agriculture, increased synergies among regulating ES under extreme climate change, and identified spatial units that may experience ES lose-lose relationships. Significance Our modeling process can support the evaluation of land management options and inform the action and support needed to achieve more desirable and equitable ES outcomes in the future.

title: Explainable machine learning decrypts the impact of compound drought and heat events on the agricultural net carbon sink: Evidences from Middle Yangtze Region, China
From organic wastes to feed, fertilizer, fuels and materials: A systems review of insect farming and biorefinery pathways in urban and agroecosystems
Diversifying cropping with vetch enhances agroecosystem services under reduced nitrogen supply: Insights from field measurements and modeling evidence
abstract: CONTEXT: Diversified cropping systems that incorporate green manures are known to improve crop productivity and deliver ecological benefits. However, their potential to sustain or enhance agroecosystem services under reduced chemical nitrogen inputs in the arid regions of northwest China remains insufficiently understood.OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to evaluate whether wheat multi-cropping with different green manure systems can maintain or enhance agroecosystem multifunctionality under reduced chemical nitrogen supply. We integrated provisioning, regulating, supporting, and economic services into a unified multi-criteria assessment framework and applied the DNDC model to explore optimal management scenarios.METHODS: A six-year field experiment was conducted in an arid irrigated region of northwest China. The main plots consisted of three nitrogen application rates: N3 (local conventional rate), N2 (20% reduction), and N1 (40% reduction). Split plots included four cropping patterns: fallow (F), common vetch (CV), a mixture of hairy vetch and common vetch (HCV), and rapeseed (R). The DNDC model was used to simulate and compare two scenarios: (1) HCV_N2 (optimized strategy) and (2) F_N3 (control).RESULTS AND CONCLUSIONS: Reducing mineral nitrogen decreased agroecosystem services, but green manuring can enhance agroecosystem services. Wheat multi-cropped mixed vetch (HCV) achieved a more balanced enhancement of agroecosystem services, and this positive effect can be further intensified by a 20% reduction in mineral nitrogen (N2). Compared with FN3, HCVN2 increased wheat yield and net ecosystem economic benefit by 20.1% and 48.1%. HCVN2 also reduced yield-scaled carbon, nitrogen, and water footprints by 6.2%, 35.7%, and 5.8%, respectively, while improving soil physical, chemical, and biological properties. As a result, HCVN2 showed the most favorable balance among provisioning, regulating, supporting, and economic services. The PLS-PM indicated that green manure was positively associated with improved soil properties, which in turn correlated with enhanced crop productivity, soil health, and economic returns while reducing environmental impacts. Scenario analysis with the DNDC modeling further suggested that wheat multi-cropping mixed vetch projected general trends of increased grain yield, reduced yield-scaled nitrogen footprint, and improved net ecosystem economic benefit across arid irrigated areas of northwest China. However, these regional projections carry inherent uncertainties related to the model's performance in capturing soil water dynamics under arid conditions. Overall, combining a 20% reduction in mineral nitrogen with wheat multi-cropping mixed vetch represents an effective strategy to enhance agroecosystem multifunctionality.SIGNIFICANCE: This strategy provides a strong agronomic and ecological foundation for transitioning toward more resilient and sustainable agricultural systems in arid irrigated regions.

title: Trust, support, and knowledge sharing: The role of social capital in responsible scaling of climate-smart agriculture
abstract: CONTEXT Accelerating the scaling of climate-smart agriculture is essential to respond to climate change while sustaining impact over time in smallholder farming systems. However, scaling agricultural innovations requires more than technical dissemination; it depends on social processes that enable farmers to exchange, adapt, and sustain knowledge in local contexts. This study examines how social capital shapes knowledge-sharing dynamics as observable indicators of early-stage scaling processes in climate-smart agriculture (CSA). OBJECTIVE This study examines how different dimensions of social capital (trust, relational closeness, and support) influence knowledge sharing as an observable behavioral indicator of early-stage scaling processes in CSA. METHODS Using survey data from 514 smallholder farmers in Climate-Smart Villages in Guatemala and Honduras, we apply regression models with robust standard errors to analyze the relationship between social capital dimensions and knowledge-sharing dynamics. Interaction effects are explored to assess how support moderates trust and relational closeness. RESULTS AND CONCLUSIONS Trust and relational closeness within community networks are consistently positive and significant predictors of knowledge sharing, while trust in organizations shows limited influence. Support received from others positively influences knowledge sharing, particularly in low-trust contexts, where it compensates for weak relational ties. Interaction effects reveal diminishing marginal returns of support as trust increases, indicating a substitution effect. Adoption of CSA practices is also positively associated with knowledge sharing. The findings demonstrate that early-stage scaling emerges from relational processes embedded in social networks. By linking social capital to knowledge-sharing dynamics, the study provides an empirical basis for operationalizing responsible scaling as a socially embedded process. These insights contribute to a more systemic understanding of how inclusive and context-sensitive scaling pathways can be enabled in agricultural systems. SIGNIFICANCE This paper advances responsible scaling research by showing how social capital can be empirically linked to observable knowledge-sharing behaviors in climate-smart agriculture. The findings offer practical guidance for AR4D programs by highlighting that scaling strategies should invest not only in technical innovations, but also in the trust, relational closeness, and support structures that enable farmers to adapt and sustain those innovations in local contexts.

title: Optimising county-level farmland allocation among crops in Northeast China under climate change and adaptive practices
Impacts of optimized irrigation and diversified crop rotations on groundwater sustainability and productivity in the North China Plain
Economic impacts and farming system responses to the first detection of coffee leaf rust in Hawaii
abstract: CONTEXT Coffee Leaf Rust (CLR) is a globally well-known plant disease that has shaped coffee production systems for decades. Hawaii's mature, high-cost specialty coffee system remained free of CLR until its first-time detection in 2020, creating a sudden biological shock. OBJECTIVE This study examines how farm system structure shapes economic impacts and adaptation pathways following the first detection of CLR into Hawaii's coffee system. METHODS Using original farm-level survey data collected from Hawaii coffee producers during 2022–2023, corresponding to the early phase of CLR spread, we classified farmers by mechanization status to capture structural heterogeneity in disease management capacity. We compare CLR exposure, management practices, cost structures, yield changes, and variations in gross margins, as well as producers' outlook and willingness to adopt CLR-resistant varieties across different mechanization-based farmer classifications. RESULTS AND CONCLUSIONS CLR is linked to significant yield losses, ranging between 31 and 56%, which, along with increased management costs across Hawaii's coffee farms, resulted in sharp declines in profitability. Non-mechanized, labor-intensive farms experienced the largest losses and negative gross margins, while partially mechanized farms diminished the magnitude of these economic impacts through more input-intensive coping strategies. Differences in outcomes and willingness to adopt CLR-resistant varieties were more closely aligned with differences in farm system characteristics rather than with reported differences in disease exposure. SIGNIFICANCE The Hawaii case shows that first-time exposure to a known plant disease can generate outsized disruption when production systems have not co-evolved with the stressor. Building resilience in perennial crop systems, therefore, requires policies and innovations that facilitate timely system transitions, rather than relying solely on intensified disease management focused on fungicide sprays.

title: Agentic Agriculture 5.0: A conceptual framework for human-artificial intelligence co-governance in wise agricultural systems
Sustainable oil palm cultivation through a One Health perspective: Linking biodiversity, ecosystem functioning and public health
abstract: CONTEXT Oil palm cultivation plays a central role in global food systems and rural economies, particularly in Southeast Asia. However, the rapid expansion of conventional monoculture plantations has been associated with deforestation, biodiversity loss, greenhouse gas emissions, ecosystem degradation, and pollution. These environmental changes may also increase the risk of zoonotic disease emergence by disrupting ecosystems and increasing human–wildlife interactions (Allen et al., 2017; Plowright et al., 2024). These interconnected environmental and health challenges highlight the need for integrated approaches that consider the relationships among ecosystem integrity, animal health, and human well-being. OBJECTIVE The present article examines oil palm cultivation through a One Health perspective in order to analyze how agricultural expansion affects biodiversity, ecosystem functioning, animal health, and public health. It also explores how sustainable management approaches, including certification systems and agroforestry-based diversification of production, can mitigate environmental degradation while improving socio-ecological resilience. METHODS The study is based on an interdisciplinary literature review integrating research from ecology, environmental sciences, epidemiology, agroforestry, and sustainability studies. The article synthesizes current knowledge on the ecological, social, and health impacts of conventional oil palm systems and evaluates sustainable alternatives such as RSPO, ISPO, and MSPO certification schemes, ecological restoration practices, and diversified agroforestry systems within a One Health conceptual framework. RESULTS AND CONCLUSIONS Conventional oil palm systems contribute to habitat fragmentation, biodiversity decline, disruption of ecosystem functions, and pollution. These changes may indirectly influence pathogen dynamics and opportunities for zoonotic spillover by altering host–pathogen interactions and ecological regulation mechanisms (Keesing et al., 2010; Johnson et al., 2020; Plowright et al., 2024). Simplified monoculture plantations generally support fewer species and weaken ecological interactions that naturally regulate disease vectors and reservoir populations. In degraded ecosystems, biodiversity loss may favor the proliferation of reservoir species that efficiently transmit pathogens, thereby altering disease dynamics and increasing spillover risks (Johnson et al., 2020). Conversely, more diverse ecosystems may contribute to disease regulation by influencing host, vector, and pathogen interactions and by maintaining ecological processes that affect pathogen transmission. However, the relationship between biodiversity and disease risk is complex and context dependent, varying among pathogens, host communities, and environmental conditions (Keesing et al., 2010; Salkeld et al., 2013). These dynamics highlight the importance of considering ecosystem integrity and ecological complexity when assessing disease emergence and transmission risks in agricultural landscapes. Agroforestry systems also enhance livelihood diversification and socio-economic resilience for rural communities. The study concludes that transforming oil palm landscapes into multifunctional socio-ecological systems is essential for reconciling agricultural productivity with environmental sustainability and public health objectives. SIGNIFICANCE This article demonstrates the relevance of the One Health framework for understanding the complex interactions linking agricultural production, biodiversity conservation, ecosystem functioning, and human health. By integrating ecological, epidemiological, and socio-economic dimensions, the study provides a comprehensive perspective on sustainable oil palm cultivation and highlights agroforestry and biodiversity-based approaches as promising pathways toward resilient tropical agricultural systems.

title: Responsible scaling for agri-food system transformation: A phased R4D framework
abstract: CONTEXT Scaling agricultural innovations is widely promoted as a pathway to transforming agri-food systems under climate change and resource pressures. Yet innovations that succeed in pilots often underperform or generate unintended consequences at scale, reflecting continued reliance on linear “pilot-to-scale” models and weak integration of responsibility in ex-ante decisions. OBJECTIVE This paper develops a practical framework to support responsible scaling for transformative impact by embedding responsibility principles—anticipation, inclusion, reflexivity, and responsiveness—within research-for-development (R4D) decision processes across the innovation lifecycle. METHODS Drawing on the literatures on scaling science, responsible innovation, and agri-food system transformation, we propose a phased R4D framework that structures scaling as a sequence of decision phases: screening, feasibility assessment, field testing, scaling pathway design, and impact assessment. The framework is illustrated with evidence from a climate-smart agriculture program, demonstrating how it supports prioritization, learning, and adaptive management under real-world constraints. RESULTS AND CONCLUSIONS The framework shows that responsible scaling is less about accelerating adoption and more about governing trade-offs across innovation pathways. Screening, feasibility, and field testing support selective learning, while pathway design and impact assessment address institutional, financial, and political economy dynamics. Together, these phases reframe scaling as an iterative decision process rather than a linear transition from pilot to expansion. SIGNIFICANCE The framework operationalizes responsible scaling as an ex-ante decision process, equipping researchers and funders with a practical tool to align innovation strategies with inclusive and sustainable transformation. It bridges conceptual debates and R4D practice while helping navigate uncertainty and political economy constraints.

title: Optimizing the sowing date partially mitigates climate risks for ratoon rice in China under future warming
Gender responsive technology assessment index: Scaling inclusive climate smart interventions in data-limited settings
abstract: CONTEXT Responsible scaling of agricultural innovations requires a nuanced understanding of technical, socioeconomic, and ecological contexts. Evaluating existing technologies using gender-responsive indicators helps inform ex-ante prioritisation when selecting among competing innovations. Although extensive knowledge exists on the gendered effects of innovations and barriers to their adoption, a comparative prioritisation framework for assessing the suitability of technology for female farmers is lacking. OBJECTIVE We develop a novel Gender Responsive Technology Assessment Index, an analytical framework to prioritise agricultural interventions for scaling based on gender-responsive technology traits. The gender responsive parameters include key welfare indicators such as employment, time requirement and drudgery. METHOD We outline a spatial prioritisation methodology to pre-inform the gender-based assessment of interventions before promoting technologies in specific geographies. This spatial prioritisation framework is designed to work in data-limited settings, where demographic and gender-disaggregated data are scarce. Additionally, we incorporate the intersectional division of labour into the index to account for social differences in responsible scaling. We consider differences in livelihood identities by focusing on ‘cultivator’ and ‘labourer’ in the segmented rural labour market. RESULT AND CONCLUSION We apply this gender responsive prioritisation framework to multiple climate-smart interventions in India. Our results show spatial differences in prioritisation outcomes for ‘machine-oriented’ and ‘non-machine-oriented’ technologies, driven by competing effects such as employment displacement and other gender-related factors. SIGNIFICANCE Our proposed framework can be adapted beyond CSA practices and scaled to evaluate inclusive and equitable technology adoption in the agri-food system. The overall methodological framework can assist in comparing existing technologies for ex-ante prioritisation and gender inclusive scaling. It can complement existing approaches of gender-inclusive responsible scaling frameworks to build equitable environments in the agri-food system.

title: Editorial Board
Adoption of digital technologies to promote animal welfare data exchange in agri-food value chains
abstract: CONTEXT The digital transformation of livestock-related Agri-Food Value Chains (AFVCs) offers substantial potential for improving Animal Health and Welfare (AHW) monitoring, traceability, and coordination. However, despite technological advancements, effective cross-actor AHW data exchange remains limited due to fragmented infrastructures and market and governance-related challenges across the chain. OBJECTIVE This study examines digital technology adoption factors for advanced AHW data exchange in AFVCs and identifies how technological, economic, and actor interaction dimensions interact to shape adoption outcomes. It aims to uncover crucial barriers, promoters, and solution approaches to develop an integrated understanding of how governance structures, incentive mechanisms, and cross-actor collaboration shape digital transformation processes in AFVCs. In particular, the study treats adoption not solely as a single-actor technology decision, but as a multi-actor coordination challenge shaped by governance, incentives, and value distribution across the AFVC. METHODS We apply a qualitative multi-method research design, analysing fourteen expert interviews and five national living labs in Germany between 2021 and 2023. The dataset covers forty-one participants including farmers, veterinarians, technology and platform providers, industry associations, and regulatory institutions. We employ a mixed-method content and network analysis to identify thematic interrelations across adoption dimensions. RESULTS AND CONCLUSIONS Our findings reveal that limited AHW data exchange is shaped less by technical deficits alone than by the combined effects of fragmented data management, limited interoperability, unclear responsibilities, high costs, uncertain returns, missing incentives, and insufficient collaboration. Actor-interaction factors, especially cooperation, trust, and intrinsic engagement, emerge as key promoters, while technological and economic enablers appear most effective when embedded in credible cooperative settings. Co-created solution approaches emphasise collaborative structures, interoperable data and platform ecosystems, transparent cost-benefit communication, financial incentives, and supportive governance frameworks. Overall, successful AHW data exchange requires technical innovation, participatory cross-actor engagement, and the creation of win-win oriented value networks, alongside integrated governance and financing strategies, and business model innovations that balance sustainability considerations, economic viability, and equity across AFVC actors. SIGNIFICANCE This study demonstrates that well-known adoption barriers and enablers also apply to AHW data exchange, and that adoption outcomes are shaped more by governance, coordination, and power relations than by techno-centric considerations alone. It offers actionable guidance for the coordination of enhanced AHW data management in AFVCs that are actor-driven, resilient, economically transparent, and technically feasible. Thus, it supports a wiser and more systems-oriented perspective on digital transformation in agriculture.

title: Biodiversity-focused nature-based solutions for climate-resilient Agri-food systems: A systematic review
abstract: Context Nature-based Solutions (NBS) are increasingly promoted as a strategy to support climate change adaptation in agricultural systems to maintain agricultural productivity while delivering co-benefits for biodiversity conservation and farmers' livelihoods. However, increasing the frequency and intensity of climate extremes, along with other management and social-ecological challenges, can affect the effectiveness of NBS. There is insufficient robust evidence on whether NBS can consistently achieve multiple objectives across different contexts. Objective This study synthesised global evidence on whether biodiversity-focused NBS in agricultural landscapes can simultaneously support biodiversity, agricultural production, and livelihoods, including under climate stress. Methods Following PRISMA guidelines, we systematically reviewed literature on biodiversity-focused NBS in agricultural landscapes. We used a mixed-methods approach to screen and synthesise qualitative and quantitative evidence on biodiversity, agricultural and livelihood outcomes, and to examine the factors associated with success, trade-offs, and NBS performance under extreme weather. Results and conclusions Across 117 NBS interventions reported in 62 cases worldwide, more than half of the reviewed cases reported simultaneous positive outcomes for biodiversity, agriculture, and livelihoods, which reveals the potential for NBS to deliver “triple-wins” under appropriate conditions. Interventions combining multiple NBS were more likely to generate positive triple outcomes than single interventions. Trade-offs and mixed outcomes were associated with socio-economic, behavioural, and biophysical constraints. Overall, the findings suggest that well-designed NBS can drive recovery and adaptive reorganisation of ecosystem function in addition to achieving goals for people at local and global scales. Significance This study provides one of the first global syntheses of “triple-win” outcomes from biodiversity-focused NBS in agricultural systems under extreme weather. It advances understanding of how NBS may contribute to climate-resilient agricultural systems and identifies the conditions under which multiple benefits are more or less likely to be achieved.

title: Investing in agroecology for resilience and sustainability: Evidence from smallholders in Rwanda
From coping to transformational CSA: Understanding systemic barriers using the iceberg model of systems thinking
Managing the water-food-energy-ecology nexus in a crop-livestock system under uncertainty: A stochastic fuzzy multi-objective approach
Effects of climate-smart agricultural practices on productivity, adaptation, and mitigation indicators: evidence from a global meta-analysis
abstract: Context Climate-smart agriculture (CSA) has been promoted globally and has potential to address three interconnected agricultural challenges: i) enhancing productivity and farm incomes; ii) building resilience and adaptive capacity to climate change; and iii) mitigating greenhouse gas emissions from farming systems. However, CSA effectiveness and impacts vary across farming systems and agroclimatic regions, and there is a lack of comprehensive global evidence synthesis. Objective The study investigated the effect of farm-level CSA technologies and management practices on the three broad CSA objectives and outcomes. Methods This study applied a three-level meta-analysis approach to synthesize findings from global studies that quantitatively investigated the effects of CSA practices on the three broad CSA objectives. Three indicators for each of the three CSA outcomes were selected to capture different but complementary CSA dimensions. Quantitative empirical studies from 2000 to 2024 were extracted and evaluated for the meta-analysis. The optimized search strategy identified 1620 paired measurements from 499 peer-reviewed articles from 66 countries and covered 42 different CSA management practices for the meta-analysis. A multi-level random effects model using standardized mean difference was used to estimate overall average effect sizes. The study checked for potential publication bias and small study effects, and applied sensitivity analysis to assess potential effects of missing studies. Results and conclusions Overall, most CSA practices improved productivity, adaptation, and mitigation indicators, although the magnitude and statistical significance of effects varied across indicators. Publication bias-adjusted estimates indicated that the effects on food consumption score and global warming potential were not statistically significant. Significance The global meta-analysis findings provide evidence and insights to guide the selection and implementation of impactful CSA strategies across global agroecological and climate zones. Such evidence and insights are not feasible from idiosyncratic national or regional meta-analysis studies.

title: Livestock roles in agroecological transitions in mixed crop-livestock systems of Tunisia
abstract: CONTEXT Despite the well-recognized role of livestock in providing goods and ecosystem services, agronomy research over the past decades has predominantly focused on plots and crops, often underestimating the contribution of animals to economic diversification within mixed farming systems. While integrated livestock-crop practices remain among the most frequently cited examples of agroecology in action, few studies assess the extent to which livestock contribute to the agroecological transition, particularly in integrated crop-livestock systems. Most of them focus on the use or non-use of these practices, particularly in mixed livestock systems. OBJECTIVE The objectives of this study are to 1) develop a method for characterizing the agroecological transition stage of crop-livestock farming systems and 2) analyze how integrating livestock into crop farming systems can promote agroecological transitions. The analysis compares farms at different stages of agroecological transition, assessed using indicators corresponding to FAO's ten elements and HLPE's thirteen principles of agroecology, across farms with contrasting levels of livestock integration. METHODS This study used data collected from a survey administered to 692 households in northwest Tunisia. Factor and cluster analyses were used to analyze the data and identify defining characteristics of crop-livestock farms at different stages of agroecological transitions, and to distill the relative importance of livestock contributions to agroecological performance, in line with agroecological principles. RESULTS AND CONCLUSION The results show that livestock play a crucial role in the agroecological transitions of Tunisian mixed farming systems. Increasing livestock numbers on mixed farms is associated with enhanced synergies among crops, trees, and animals, particularly through nutrient recycling and the utilization of residues as livestock feed. However, challenges persist regarding knowledge co-creation, recycling and connectivity, and land and resource governance in landscapes with mixed farming systems. SIGNIFICANCE The study addresses the discrepancy between global frameworks and on-the-ground realities by integrating localized analyses of farming and livestock systems with broader principles of agroecology. While integrating livestock into farming systems in dryland areas can be considered a transformative pathway toward sustainable agriculture, the findings underscore the significance of social networks and connectivity between producers and consumers, governance, and knowledge sharing in promoting agroecological practices.

A review of agricultural peat soil models and the implications for sustainable peatland use
abstract: CONTEXT Drained peatlands in Europe, predominantly used as permanent pasture for dairy production, are increasingly debated due to their high impact on climate change and biodiversity loss. Models are tools often used to aid decision making, because they assess consequences of changing farm management in socio-economic and environmental terms. OBJECTIVE To create an overview of models used to assess interventions in peat soils used for dairy farming, and to determine how they inform sustainable peatland use. METHODS We performed a systematic literature review to identify the type of models developed; sustainability aspects covered; and the management options or interventions studied. RESULTS AND CONCLUSIONS In total, 33 models were found. Models differed in their scale of analysis and predominantly focused on environmental themes, rather than social or economic themes. The most studied intervention was changing water tables. Increasing water tables resulted in a shift towards more diverse farming systems. Model outcomes showed a decrease in GHG emissions with increasing water tables, indicating that conventional dairy farming with water tables beyond −50 cm conflicts with achieving environmental targets. With increasing water tables, extensive dairy farming or shifting to paludiculture were modelled as potential alternatives. Yet, a more comprehensive understanding of the alternative systems and more insight into their socio-economic and environmental performance is lacking. SIGNIFICANCE Current models are limited in informing sustainable peatland use, addressing limited sustainability dimensions and exploring few alternatives to currents dairy production. Future models should adopt a more holistic approach, by incorporating multiple objectives, sustainability dimensions and scales, to better inform sustainable peatland management.

title: Too late for responsibility? Dialogic prompts for responsible decision-making in agricultural research for development
abstract: Context Despite efforts for agricultural innovations to reach scale, they often do not achieve socially and environmentally desirable impacts. In response, several frameworks, methods, and tools have been developed to promote Responsible Scaling. However, they do not integrate responsible decision-making throughout the entire trajectory of agricultural research for development (AR4D). Anticipatory planning and reflexive learning opportunities remain limited, and innovations risk being designed in isolation from intended users and dynamically changing contexts. Objective This paper serves as a call to action for researchers and practitioners to consider dimensions of Responsible Innovation – anticipation, inclusion, reflexivity and responsiveness (AIRR) – across the entire innovation and scaling trajectory. Methods Based on a narrative literature review, we introduce a novel Responsible Innovation and Scaling framework (RIS) as well as exemplary methodologies, methods, and dialogic prompts that help embed RIS across AR4D. Results The novel RIS framework consists of four iteratively interacting phases: collaborative ideation and development, flexible innovation packaging, co-implementation, and dynamic evaluation. AIRR dimensions inform the selection of exemplary methodologies and methods and the use of dialogic prompts across these phases. We acknowledge that putting RIS into action depends on several conditions, i.e.: supportive leadership, interdependent capacities, and spaces of collective learning, such as communities of practice. Significance The RIS framework, relevant methodologies, methods, and dialogic prompts are intended to help researchers and practitioners interrogate assumptions, identify trade-offs, foster inclusion and flexibility, and navigate power dynamics to guide responsible decision-making across innovation and scaling processes in AR4D.

title: Quantifying the water–energy–food–carbon nexus and carbon-emission transmission pathways in grain production: Evidence from 340 Chinese cities
A review of digital decision support systems in European cereal crop production: Applications, opportunities, challenges, and critical success factors
abstract: CONTEXT As technology evolves, digital decision support systems (DSSs) are increasingly implemented worldwide. This is especially true in agriculture, where a growing global population and environmental pressures are leading to a situation where more food must be produced whilst environmental sustainability remains at the forefront. Many digital DSSs have been created for cereal crop production, however implementation of these DSSs remains limited. OBJECTIVE This review examines the application, opportunities, and challenges of these systems within European rainfed cereal crop production, aiming to identify how recent advancements have the potential to enhance specific agricultural applications, including variety selection, soil moisture prediction, and pest management, and to identify gaps and areas for improvement in the development of DSSs. METHODS A review of the literature was conducted. To ensure that future developed DSSs achieve high adoption rates, this review sets out critical success factors in the context of European rainfed cereal crop production. RESULTS AND CONCLUSIONS Findings reveal that DSSs are widely available but in many cases currently lack high adoption rates. A system must be flexible, accessible, and highly relevant to local conditions for adoption to occur. However, the most essential factor for overcoming current adoption plateaus is the shifting from a technology-first approach to one that involves the end-user in the design process. SIGNIFICANCE The implementation of these factors by DSS developers can lead to delivering tangible value to the cereal production sector, helping end-users to move towards making data-driven decisions.

title: The environmental impacts of the scale of circularity in food systems
abstract: CONTEXT Reconnecting nutrient cycles is essential to reduce environmental impacts of food systems. It remains unknown how circularity at different spatial scales affects nitrogen (N) losses, inputs, and greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. OBJECTIVE We investigated impacts of reconnecting nutrient cycles in the Dutch food system at national or more local, i.e., provincial level, and assessed effects on N flows, N losses and GHG emissions. METHODS We adapted the agroecological food systems optimization model FOODSOM, by integrating soil type- and groundwater level-specific N transfer coefficients, and applied this extended model to evaluate N flows of Dutch circular food systems in a spatially explicit manner. We assessed how varying degrees of provincial food sourcing, and consequently local nutrient cycling, affected land use, N losses, and GHG emissions. The assumed diet followed national food-based dietary guidelines. RESULTS AND CONCLUSIONS Compared to the current state with substantial trade, a domestic circular food system in the Netherlands reduced land use by 26–35%, N inputs two-thirds, NH 3 emissions ∼80%, NO x emissions ∼50%, N leaching and runoff 19–38%, and GHG emissions 64–86%. High degrees of provincial food sourcing increased N losses and GHG emissions, because this required the use of less suitable peatland and wet soils, and more ruminants in urbanized provinces. However, 50–75% of consumed N could be sourced locally within provinces without significantly increasing impacts compared with national sourcing. SIGNIFICANCE Nutrient circularity substantially reduced N losses and GHG emissions. Food sourcing at provincial rather than national scale did not further reduce N losses and GHG emissions. In countries with more varied production conditions, benefits and drawbacks of local sourcing are likely more pronounced.

title: Diversifying tropical agroforestry: High-value understory crops in rubber and coconut systems
abstract: CONTEXT Tropical agriculture faces increasing challenges in sustaining production and rural livelihoods while addressing climate change, biodiversity loss, soil degradation, and resource limitations. Multi-strata agroforestry systems integrating perennial overstory crops with high-value understory species offer a promising pathway for climate-smart intensification and sustainable tropical agriculture. OBJECTIVE This review synthesizes evidence from multi-strata agroforestry systems combining major overstory crops, including Hevea brasiliensis , Cocos nucifera , and Areca catechu , with high-value understory crops such as spices, beverage, and medicinal plants. We develop a trait-based framework linking overstory characteristics, ecological interactions, management strategies, and ecosystem multifunctionality. METHODS A comprehensive literature synthesis was conducted using Web of Science Core Collection, Scopus, and Google Scholar, focusing on productivity, ecosystem services, resource-use efficiency, management practices, and socioeconomic outcomes. The evidence was organized around overstory–understory interactions, climate resilience, ecosystem services, productivity, and adoption challenges. RESULTS AND CONCLUSIONS Multi-strata agroforestry systems enhance carbon (C) storage, biodiversity, soil functions, and land-use efficiency compared with monocultures, with land equivalent ratios (LER) frequently exceeding 1.0. Reported evidence indicates that agroforestry systems can increase C storage by 20–50%, improve soil organic carbon (SOC) stocks by 10–20% compared with monocultures, and reduce midday air and soil temperatures by approximately 3–5 °C and 2–4 °C, respectively. High-value understory crops further enhance productivity and income diversification, with LER values commonly ranging from 1.2 to 1.8 and exceeding 2.0 in some shade-adapted crops. However, outcomes remain context-dependent due to competition for light, water, and nutrients, as well as potential pest and disease risks. Optimized performance depends on complementary species selection, canopy regulation, and adaptive soil fertility management. Key knowledge gaps remain in long-term productivity, C sequestration dynamics, resource competition thresholds, and socioeconomic barriers. SIGNIFICANCE Diversified overstory–understory agroforestry systems represent a nature-based solution for developing resilient tropical landscapes by integrating agricultural productivity, biodiversity conservation, ecosystem services, and climate change mitigation.

title: When the advisor is an algorithm: governing agri-food knowledge in the age of AI and misinformation
abstract: CONTEXT Artificial intelligence is becoming an important interface through which farmers, advisors and policymakers access agricultural knowledge, while misinformation increasingly circulates through the same digital channels. OBJECTIVE This Perspective develops the concept of agri-food knowledge governance to explain how AI-mediated advice and misinformation create shared challenges of knowledge validation, contextual relevance and accountability. METHODS The paper conceptually synthesises literature on agricultural knowledge and innovation systems, digital agriculture governance, agri-food misinformation and the epistemology of testimony. RESULTS AND CONCLUSIONS The synthesis identifies six governance functions: provenance and traceability, context fidelity, human epistemic intermediation, plural authority and data rights, resilience and literacy, and accountability and redress. These functions shift attention beyond technical accuracy toward locally valid, contestable and accountable agricultural advice. They become especially important as AI systems move from generating recommendations to executing decisions. SIGNIFICANCE Agri-food knowledge governance extends existing agricultural knowledge-system approaches by explicitly addressing epistemic authority, contextual validity and accountability. It provides a framework for evaluating and governing AI-enabled advisory systems while preserving plural and locally grounded sources of agricultural knowledge.

title: Land-use intensification reshapes plant diversity and soil nutrient dynamics across mountainous rural landscapes
Optimal landscape to sustainable cocoa culture in the context of epidemiological control of cocoa swollen shoot virus: A theoretical approach
abstract: CONTEXT Cocoa swollen shoot virus (CSSV) remains the most destructive viral disease affecting cocoa in West Africa, with ecological and economic repercussions. Since the virus is specialized to cocoa and disperse locally through mealybugs vectors, landscape structure could play a crucial role in determining epidemic outcomes. OBJECTIVES This study aimed to assess how landscape structure influences CSSV spread and economic returns, to identify landscape structures that reconcile epidemiological control with profitability. METHODS The spatially and temporally explicit landsepi model was parameterized for the CSSV pathosys tem using literature-derived data and calibrated through Approximate Bayesian Computation based on field observations. The model was then used to compare landscape mosaics varying in cocoa (host) and coffee (non-host) proportions and spatial aggregation, under contrasting disease pressure, economic, and yield scenarios over a 20-year period. RESULTS AND CONCLUSIONS Epidemiologically, long-term cocoa survival improved in fragmented landscapes, with optimal outcomes below 40% cocoa under low disease pressure and below 20% under high pressure. However, these compositions reduced total system income. Economically, cocoa-dominated landscapes remained profitable under low disease pressure. Under high disease pressure, profitability persisted only in the short (4–5 years) to medium term (12–13 years), depending on cocoa–coffee gains differences. Over longer periods, profitability declined unless profits were accumulated, indicating that short-term benefits only partly offset long-term losses. SIGNIFICANCE Collective, landscape-scale diversification emerges as a promising strategy to contain CSSV while sustaining cocoa production. By jointly considering disease pressure and landscape structure, stakeholders can design context specific landscape mosaic that reconcile epidemic control with economic profitability.
