Beyond One-Size-Fits-All: Using Farming Typologies to Navigate the NUE-Yield-GHG Nexus in Indian Cereal Systems
abstract: CONTEXT Intensive cereal production systems face the dual challenge of increasing food production while reducing environmental impacts, particularly greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions associated with nitrogen fertilizer use. Nitrogen use efficiency (NUE) is a critical lever linking crop productivity, input-use-efficiency, soil health, and climate mitigation. However, wide heterogeneity in farming practices across smallholder systems complicates the effectiveness of uniform nutrient management recommendations. Understanding how different farming typologies shape the nexus between NUE, crop yield, and GHG emissions is essential for advancing sustainable intensification in agriculture. OBJECTIVE The study evaluates the interlinkages between nitrogen use efficiency, crop productivity, and GHG emissions across diverse farming typologies for paddy, wheat, and maize, and identifies typology-specific pathways and policy-relevant strategies that can simultaneously improve yields, enhance NUE, and reduce GHG emissions. METHODS The analysis uses cost of cultivation data from over 16,000 farm households across India. Farmers were classified into distinct farming typologies using a weighted K-Modes clustering approach based on water management, tillage practices, residue management, crop varieties, and fertilizer use. GHG emissions were estimated using the CCAFS Mitigation Options Tool. The relationships between NUE, crop yield, and emissions were examined across typologies to identify dominant production pathways and performance trade-offs. RESULTS AND CONCLUSIONS Results show that a substantial proportion of farmers operate outside the optimal NUE “safe operating zone” (i.e. 50–90% NUE) across all three cereals. Between 33% and 49% of farmers fall into low-NUE/low-yield conditions, indicating systemic inefficiencies rather than isolated management failures. Two dominant unsustainable pathways emerge: nitrogen-surplus systems that achieve moderate to high yields but exhibit low NUE and high emission intensity, and soil-mining systems characterized by very high NUE but inadequate nitrogen inputs, low yields, and long-term risks to soil fertility. In contrast, balanced management typologies, featuring improved varieties, residue incorporation, conservation tillage, and efficient water management, achieve competitive yields with lower emissions. These findings demonstrate that pursuing yield or NUE in isolation is counterproductive and that balanced, site-specific nutrient management is essential for sustainable outcomes. SIGNIFICANCE The study highlights the decisive role of farming typologies in shaping the NUE-Yield-GHG nexus and demonstrates the limitations of one-size-fits-all nutrient recommendations. The typology framework provides a practical and scalable tool for identifying “win–win” systems and high-risk pathways, enabling targeted, site-specific interventions to maximize synergies and minimize trade-offs. Policy implications include the need for nutrient rationalization in surplus systems, moderate intensification and soil restoration in soil-mining systems, and enabling institutional support such as soil testing, extension services, and appropriate subsidy structures. By guiding transitions toward balanced management typologies, this approach supports sustainable intensification, climate mitigation, and food security objectives in India and offers relevance for smallholder cereal systems globally.

title: Stakeholder evaluation of livestock scenarios in Switzerland using value-based multi-criteria analysis
abstract: CONTEXT,Agri-food systems are multi-functional, leading to unavoidable trade-offs when attempting to transform them for greater sustainability. Addressing these trade-offs while considering food security and balancing social, environmental, and economic welfare could unlock opportunities for meaningful transformation.,OBJECTIVE,This study aims to reveal the unavoidable trade-offs in Swiss livestock production and understand how different stakeholders in the system wish to address these trade-offs.,METHODS,We applied value-focused Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis (MCDA) to assess four contrasting scenarios for the future of Swiss livestock production. These scenarios are business as usual, efficiency, sufficiency, and consistency. We based the relative assessment on (1) the system predictions on 14 key objectives that the sector should fulfill and (2) stakeholder preferences on how to prioritize these objectives. To understand stakeholder preferences, we collected weighting data from 20 representatives across three political clusters: green, conservative, and liberal.,RESULTS AND CONCLUSIONS,Our findings indicate strong disagreement among stakeholders regarding the importance of animal welfare and domestic food production. However, despite these differences, the sufficiency and consistency scenarios were found to be more satisfactory for all stakeholders compared to the business as usual and efficiency scenarios. These results highlight potential pathways for more widely accepted policy interventions.,SIGNIFICANCE,By illustrating key trade-offs and stakeholder preferences, this study provides valuable insights for policymaking in Swiss livestock production and beyond. The findings can help guide the development of more sustainable and broadly supported agricultural policies, e.g. prioritizing goals for reorienting subsidies.

title: Do precision land management technologies improve farm efficiency? Evidence from laser land levelling in India
abstract: Context: The Indian agriculture system is increasingly constrained by resources and climate vulnerability, with rapid groundwater depletion. This is creating an urgency for adoption of resource-efficient agricultural technologies to address sustainability challenges in intensively irrigated systems. Laser land levelling (LLL) has emerged as a prominent resource and precision land management technology. Objective: The study tries to examine the key determinants of LLL adoption and its impact on paddy productivity in Punjab. Secondly, the study also evaluates the technical efficiency of LLL in paddy production. Finally, we examine heterogeneity in technical efficiency outcomes separately for marginal landholders to assess whether the efficiency gains from LLL adoption vary by farm size. Methods: Primary survey data is collected from 885 farmers from 12 districts in Punjab, India. The sample comprises of 527 (60%) adopters and 358 (40%) non-adopters of LLL. We use a probit model to identify the key drivers of adoption and derive the inverse mills ratio for correcting the sample selection bias. The, we use propensity score matching to estimate causal impact of LLL adoption on paddy yield. Finally, we apply the stochastic production frontier framework with sample-selection correction to evaluate the technical efficiency levels. Results and Conclusions: The findings highlight that LLL adoption increases paddy yield by 2.64 quintals/acre. Efficiency estimates show that adopters achieve approximately 3% higher technical efficiency compared to non-adopters. Moreover, adoption decisions are influenced by structural and asset-related factors, including education, landholding size, and ownership of tractors and pumpsets. Notably, efficiency gains are larger for the marginal farmers, suggesting that smaller landholders may have greater scope of improvements from LLL adoption. Significance: This study contributes two fold: It provides a new empirical evidence on the determinants and impact of LLL adoption in paddy cultivation. Secondly, we develop an integrated econometric framework to address selection bias and evaluate efficiency outcomes of LLL adoption. The study highlights the multidimensional benefits of LLL in enhancing productivity and efficiency, supporting its promotion as a climate-smart technology in improving resource-use efficiency and reducing groundwater stress in rice-based farming systems in India.

title: Intercropping increases crop diversity - but do the effects persist after intercropping abandonment? Insights from a national farmer network
abstract: Context Intercropping, growing multiple plant species simultaneously on the same field, provides clear ecological benefits in experimental settings. However, its implementation in real farms and its impacts on crop diversity and composition at the cropping-system level remain understudied. Objective This study aimed at assessing how intercropping influences cropping-system diversity. Methods Data from the French DEPHY network, > 2000 farms monitored since 2010, were used to track changes in crop diversity and composition in different crop families before, during, and after intercropping was adopted. We analysed 414 cropping systems, both conventional and organic. Results and conclusions Intercropping resulted in a significant increase of 52% in species richness, 22% in Shannon diversity, and 9% in evenness at the cropping-system level, mainly due to an increase of 96% in the proportion of legumes and reduced proportion of 19% of cereals. Farmers intercropped mainly cereals with legumes, representing 90% of mixtures in organic, and 66% in conventional. Of the 414 systems studied, 40% abandoned intercropping, which resulted in a decrease in diversity and the proportion of legumes. In 92% of the species mixtures, some species were lost when intercropping was abandoned, especially legumes and minor crops. Significance These results demonstrate that intercropping can diversify cropping systems effectively under real farming conditions, particularly by reintroducing legumes, but its long-term benefits on diversity are limited by the low persistence of species after intercropping is abandoned. By providing new evidence on how farmers adopt and abandon intercropping over time, this study provides insights for designing policies and advisory strategies that support biodiversity-friendly farming.

Machine learning-enhanced 4DVar assimilation for winter wheat yield estimation
abstract: Context Accurate crop yield estimation is crucial for ensuring food security, promoting sustainable agriculture, and optimizing management practices. However, integrating remote sensing data with crop models remains challenging, largely due to the inability of traditional data assimilation methods to adequately represent complex, spatiotemporally variable error covariance structures. Objective This study aims to improve crop yield prediction by addressing the persistent challenge of error covariance specification in data assimilation. We seek to establish a more rigorous and adaptive approach for determining error covariance, thereby enhancing the accuracy and reliability of yield estimates. Methods We developed a machine learning–enhanced four-dimensional variational data assimilation algorithm (ML-4DVar), in which ML models (Random Forest, Extreme Gradient Boosting, and Long Short-Term Memory) dynamically estimate error covariance matrices for both crop model outputs and remote sensing observations. Comparative experiments were conducted against conventional 4DVar and Ensemble Kalman Filter (EnKF) approaches for yield prediction. Results and conclusions ML-4DVar substantially improved predictive skill relative to benchmark methods, achieving a Spearman's correlation coefficient of 0.92, an RMSE of 369.29 kg/ha, and an R 2 of 0.86. The results demonstrate that incorporating machine learning into 4DVar provides a more flexible representation of uncertainties and improves the fusion of remote sensing and model information for yield estimation. Significance The proposed ML-4DVar framework offers a promising pathway for advancing data–model fusion in agricultural monitoring. Future research may extend this approach across regions, crop types, and higher-resolution data streams to support scalable, policy-relevant agricultural forecasting under global change.

title: Nitrogenius 2: A web-based decision support system for nitrogen governance and learning
abstract: CONTEXT The Netherlands faces an acute nitrogen governance challenge. Intensive agriculture and industry cause freshwater eutrophication, terrestrial acidification, and climate change, while most Natura 2000 areas exceed critical deposition thresholds. A key barrier is limited shared understanding of how nitrogen flows connect ecological, economic, and social processes. OBJECTIVE This paper presents the design and evaluation of Nitrogenius 2, a web-based decision support system and serious game that makes nitrogen system dynamics, trade-offs, and stakeholder interdependencies explicit and accessible. METHODS Nitrogenius 2 integrates activity-based emission accounting, spatially explicit deposition modelling across a 1520-cell grid of the Netherlands, and composite socio-economic indicators within a turn-based simulation covering 2025–2035, incorporating 137 policy measures across four stakeholder roles. Evaluations included a validation test against official Dutch reference data and a classroom deployment at two Dutch universities ( n = 52), complemented by a comparative analysis of environmental-economic trade-offs. RESULTS AND CONCLUSIONS All modelled values fell within 3% of official reference values. Over 80% of participants agreed the system improved their understanding of stakeholder roles and policy complexity, though lower scores on emission-deposition items indicate scope for improving interface transparency. Comparative analysis identified “Switch to Organic Dairy” as the most cost-effective agricultural measure, while targeted buyouts yielded the largest improvement in Natura 2000 protection. SIGNIFICANCE Nitrogenius 2 is an open-source platform bridging the analytical rigor of decision support systems with the participatory strengths of serious games. Its modular architecture supports adaptation to other geographic contexts and environmental policy domains.

Beyond the trees: Exploring the determinants of intercrop management intensity in smallholder immature rubber systems in Thailand
abstract: CONTEXT Ensuring natural rubber production while minimizing negative impacts in rubber-based cropping systems is a major challenge that must be addressed from the immature period, which typically lasts 6–7 years before tapping begins. Management during the immature period is critical to ensure optimal plantation long-term development. Intercropping is widely practiced in the inter-rows during the first four years after planting, with varying levels of management intensity. While previous studies have examined the adoption of intercropping in immature rubber plantations, what determines intercrop management intensity remains unexplored. OBJECTIVE The aim of this study was to explore the determinants of intercrop management intensity in smallholder immature rubber plantations, focusing on three technical operations: planting density, mineral fertilizer rates, and herbicide use. METHODS Semi-directive interviews were conducted with 73 farmers managing rubber plantations intercropped with cassava in Buriram province, pineapple in Rayong province, or upland rice in Trang province, Thailand. Based on a literature review, 38 variables representing the external and internal farm context, as well as other livelihood strategies, were identified as potential determinants of intercrop management intensity. Random forest algorithms were used to select the most contributing variables for each technical operation, and Classification and Regression Trees were then applied to assess how these variables shaped management intensity. RESULTS AND CONCLUSION Twelve variables emerged as determinants of the technical operations studied. They were linked to the external context of the farm (i.e. soil problems, difficulty of weed species management, and financial support for rubber replanting), the internal context (e.g., savings, tractor ownership) and livelihood strategies (other crop areas). Each determinant was associated with only one technical operation, and its effects were mostly not distinguishable across intercropping systems. Some determinants, such as participation in training programs on intercropping, may represent promising entry points for promoting the transition toward more sustainable rubber-based systems, with potential implications for policy design and implementation. SIGNIFICANCE By identifying factors associated with intercrop management intensity, this exploratory study provides critical insights for understanding the levers and barriers to adopting and scaling more sustainable practices in immature rubber-based systems. These findings can inform both local extension services and broader policy initiatives aimed at improving sustainability in smallholder rubber production.
